messages.subject: gdistsamp - issues with covariates and starting values when fitting hazard-rate detection function
parts:
Dear fellow unmarked enthusiasts,

I am attempting to compute density estimates of migratory land birds using the "gdistsamp" function within unmarked. I surveyed 12 transects, 18 times using distance sampling. I am running into issues when fitting a model to the data.  I keep getting the error everyone seems to dread: 

Warning message:
In gdistsamp(~1, ~1, ~1, BHNWumf, keyfun = "hazard", output = "density",  :
  Hessian is singular. Try using fewer covariates and supplying starting values.

I get the error when trying to fit a hazard function through all of my data at once and I also get it when attempting to fit it through data for one transect. I did get it to fit with one of my 12 transects, but I am a bit confused as to why I get this error when trying to fit the null model to another transect's data.

When I try to provide starting values, I also get an error. I may be missing something obvious, but I cannot seem to wrap my head around this error when I am not using covariates in the model. I have been reading forum posts for days now, but cannot seem to find a solution. Any tips and or suggestions are welcome. Thanks!

Cheers,
Tim

Here's the code I am using on a Mac OS and R Studio Version 0.98.1056. Because this is for each transect, siteCovs are not necessary. I did standardize my covariates (using the scale function) before building the unmarkedFrameGDS.

cutpt = as.numeric(c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 50))

#Bombay Hook data

windtran <- windBHNWtestnew #wind covariate data
skytran <- skyBHNWtestnew #sky covariate data
temptran <- tempBHNWtestnew #temp covariate data

BHNWumf = unmarkedFrameGDS(y=distsBHNW, 
                       numPrimary=18,
                       #siteCovs=sitecovsBHNW,

parts:
hi Tim,
 
 3 of the parameters are clearly at the boundary of the parameter space (availability = 16.5 means phi = 1) and the other two are also looking a bit strange.
 I suggest fitting the half-normal model and see what happens (that has 1 fewer parameter).
 Another possibility is that there is no evidence of temporary emigration (i.e., phi = 1) which means you will never get valid SEs out because the likelihood is over-conditioned. 
 In that case you should "stack" your data which we've talked about on the listserve before. That is, take the primary periods for each site and treat them as new sites.

 hope this helps
regards
andy

hi Tim,

 It looks like you have bad starting values here which seems to be a common occurrence.  At some point we'll have to come up with good ideas for default starting values.
 In any case, I think you should play around with different values and see what happens.

 For estimating density across years I think stacking the data provides an ideal solution. Just include year as a covariate. With the stacked data structure it would be a "site covariate".

 Is it correct that you sampled over 2 years and you have 18 samples of the same points in year 1 and 15 samples of the points in year 2?  And they're the same points sampled on different days?

andy

Hi Andy,

I'll try playing around with starting values and stacking the data. Yes, the same sites were sampled each year. We tried sampling sites every four days, but that wasn't possible due to inclement weather. So, the first year of the study, we had 18 sampling periods and only 15 for the second year.

In the end, we are trying to see how our migrant densities on the ground compare to weather radar observations from each site.

Cheers,
Tim
On Sat, Dec 13, 2014 at 10:20 AM, Jeffrey Royle <jar...@gmail.com> wrote:

hi Tim,

 It looks like you have bad starting values here which seems to be a common occurrence.  At some point we'll have to come up with good ideas for default starting values.
 In any case, I think you should play around with different values and see what happens.

 For estimating density across years I think stacking the data provides an ideal solution. Just include year as a covariate. With the stacked data structure it would be a "site covariate".

 Is it correct that you sampled over 2 years and you have 18 samples of the same points in year 1 and 15 samples of the points in year 2?  And they're the same points sampled on different days?

andy


On Fri, Dec 12, 2014 at 6:15 PM, Tim Schreckengost <timschre...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Andy,

Thanks for the swift reply! I have a few follow-up questions and comments.

When I attempt to fit the halfnorm function in the null model, I get the following error.

> m1 <- gdistsamp(~1, ~1, ~1, BHNWumf, keyfun = "halfnorm", output="density", unitsOut = "ha", K = 50)
Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se, ...) : 
  initial value in 'vmmin' is not finite

I was reading through the "stacking data" threads, therefore I have a basic understanding of the process. I did not sample the each site the same number of times each season (18 primary periods in season 1 and 15 primary periods in season 2). Should I just fill in the extra sampling periods with NAs? Also, I need to compute mean densities on a per year basis (so migrants/ha/visit for each year). With that said, does stacking the data make sense? Thanks!

Cheers,
Tim

On Thursday, December 11, 2014 10:12:45 PM UTC-5, Jeffrey Royle wrote:
hi Tim,
 
 3 of the parameters are clearly at the boundary of the parameter space (availability = 16.5 means phi = 1) and the other two are also looking a bit strange.
 I suggest fitting the half-normal model and see what happens (that has 1 fewer parameter).
 Another possibility is that there is no evidence of temporary emigration (i.e., phi = 1) which means you will never get valid SEs out because the likelihood is over-conditioned. 
 In that case you should "stack" your data which we've talked about on the listserve before. That is, take the primary periods for each site and treat them as new sites.

 hope this helps
regards
andy
